preamble: The perimeter letters spell out an appropriate message, but these letters are not included in the subsidiary indications in the relevant clues.

clue.text: Dissidents before joining irregular movements

parts.note: ere is an old word for before
tics are involuntary twitches

explanation.surface: Rebels signing up to a ragged protest campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: Per the preamble, the opening H sits on the grid's edge and gets no wordplay; it starts the border message HAPPY NEW YEAR FROM PASQUALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Heretics hold opinions at odds with accepted doctrine, which makes them rebels against orthodoxy.

clue.text: Old pike or luce

wordplay.note: ged is a Scottish and northern word for the pike, and luce is another old name for the same fish

explanation.surface: An elderly fish, whichever of its names you call it by.
explanation.walkthrough: The A starts the edge message, so the wordplay covers only the rest; 'pike or luce' gives two names for one fish so the solver can home in on the obscure third, GED.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone aged has lived many years, so the word is a plain synonym for elderly.

clue.text: One of the three for all the feeling that arouses pity

wordplay.words: One of the three for all
wordplay.note: Athos is one of Dumas's Three Musketeers, whose motto is 'all for one and one for all'

explanation.surface: A musketeer swept up in a moving, pitiable mood.
explanation.walkthrough: The P on the border belongs to the message and is not clued. 'One for all' recalls the Musketeers' motto, so 'one of the three' is a musketeer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathos is the quality in art or life that stirs sympathy and sorrow in an onlooker.

clue.text: A run with a high-arcing ball going up on a curve

parts.note: taken as written
R is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for a run

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means read from the bottom, so the letters come out backwards

parts.note: the article, added on
a lob is a ball hit or thrown high in an arc
the article, with the upturned ball sitting on it in the down entry

explanation.surface: A cricketer scoring a run off a lofted ball that loops through the air.
explanation.walkthrough: The P on the border is the message's and gets no wordplay. 'On' places the upturned ball above the final A in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A parabola is the symmetrical open curve traced by a projectile such as a thrown ball.

clue.text: Arrest mad, unruly boss employed by railway

indicators.note: unruly things refuse to stay in order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A call to detain a crazed, out-of-control railway manager.
explanation.walkthrough: The initial Y is a border letter of the message, so the anagram supplies only the other nine letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardmaster supervises a railway marshalling yard, directing the shunting of wagons and trains.

clue.text: A man who painted Japanese city

parts.note: taken as written
Francisco Goya, the Spanish painter, is the man in question

explanation.surface: An artist who once painted a scene of a Japanese city.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading N belongs to the border message and is not clued; the rest is A plus the Spanish painter Goya.
explanation.definitionFit: Nagoya is a major industrial port on Honshu, the country's fourth-largest urban area.

clue.text: English girl collects grey marine plant

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for English

indicators.note: to collect is to gather in, so one piece takes another inside it

parts.note: a lass is a girl
gr. is a dictionary abbreviation for grey

explanation.surface: An English girl gathering grey seaweed on the shore.
explanation.walkthrough: The first E is the border letter and gets no wordplay, so the English E clued here is the second one.
explanation.definitionFit: Eelgrass is a flowering seagrass with long ribbon leaves that grows in shallow coastal water.

clue.text: Most wise and godly person over a long period of time

indicators.note: one thing spread over another covers it on both sides, enclosing it

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for saint
ages means a very long time

explanation.surface: Praising someone as both wisest and most saintly over a lifetime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most wise and godly' reads as one description, but 'and' is the hinge between the definition and the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Sage means wise, so its superlative describes the wisest of a group.

clue.text: Feasts a non-believer endlessly rejected?

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off
something rejected is sent back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: taken as written
a pagan is a non-believer, here missing its last letter

explanation.surface: Feasts at which an unbeliever was turned away, never-endingly.
explanation.walkthrough: The final E is a border letter and is not clued. Agapae is the plural of agape, used here in its sense of a feast rather than love.
explanation.definitionFit: Agapae were the communal love feasts held by early Christians alongside the Eucharist.

clue.text: Stop loan

wordplay.note: to stop something is to end it

explanation.walkthrough: The L sits on the border and belongs to the message. 'Stop loan' reads like a banker's order, but 'loan' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To loan something is to let someone use it temporarily, the same act as lending it.

clue.text: Look after good worker after greeting all around

indicators.note: after means coming later, so the piece before this word is placed behind the one following it

parts.note: hi is an informal greeting
G is the abbreviation for good
a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand
lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: Caring for a valued employee after saying hello to everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The W ends on the border, so the wordplay stops at LO. Each 'after' puts the piece before it later in the answer, so the pieces assemble in reverse clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: To search high and low is to search everywhere, so the phrase means in every place.

clue.text: Plane, Irish-American, carrying British

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it, so one piece holds another

parts.note: IR is the abbreviation for Irish
US for American, as in US citizen
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.surface: An airliner with an Irish-American crew flying a Briton.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening A is a border letter of the message and is not clued; the wordplay builds only IRBUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Airbus is the European aircraft maker whose name is used for any of its airliners.

clue.text: Rub old goo around, type of fluid for the body

definitions.text: type of fluid for the body

indicators.note: around here means scattered about, so the letters are moved into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Massaging old gunk into the skin with some bodily fluid.
explanation.walkthrough: The last P is a border letter, so the nine-letter anagram supplies everything but it.
explanation.definitionFit: A blood group, such as A or O, classifies blood by the antigens on its red cells.

clue.text: Going around tug, observed a non-paying passenger

indicators.note: to go around something is to encircle it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: saw is the past tense of see, to observe
to tow is to tug or pull along
taken as written

explanation.surface: Spotting someone travelling free while circling a tugboat.
explanation.walkthrough: The final Y belongs to the border message and gets no wordplay. 'Tug' reads as a boat, but it is the verb meaning to pull.
explanation.definitionFit: A stowaway hides aboard a ship or plane to travel without paying the fare.

clue.text: Partner without children sitting by river

parts.note: s.p. stands for sine prole, Latin for without issue, used in family trees
the Ouse is a river in England

explanation.surface: A childless partner relaxing on a riverbank.
explanation.walkthrough: S.P. is the genealogist's abbreviation for dying without children; the Ouse is one of several English rivers of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: A spouse is a husband or wife, the person one is married to.

clue.text: Worship of the Devil — a transgression shown up after the Last Day!

parts.note: Saturday, abbreviated SAT, is the last day of the week
taken as written

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means bottom to top, so the letters read backwards

parts.note: a sin is a transgression

explanation.surface: Devil-worship revealed as a sin come Judgement Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Last Day' suggests Judgement Day, but here it is Saturday, the week's final day. The M at the bottom is a border letter and is not clued.
explanation.definitionFit: Satanism is the veneration of Satan, so it is literally the worship of the Devil.

clue.text: Small protest message against O'Shanter

parts.note: a placard's slogan, as in 'Ban the Bomb', demands a ban
a tam-o'-shanter is a Scottish bonnet, so O'Shanter completes TAM

explanation.surface: A little protest slogan against Tam o'Shanter, Burns's hero.
explanation.walkthrough: The bonnet is called a tam-o'-shanter or just tam, so O'Shanter is cheekily the second half of a name standing for its first.
explanation.definitionFit: Bantam is a small breed of chicken, and by extension anything diminutive or lightweight.

clue.text: Wickedness is evident after Mass — that is undermining church

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for mass
taken as written
CH is the abbreviation for church
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: Sin on show after the church service, with a churchgoer subverting the faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' is the physics abbreviation, not the service. In a down entry, undermining a piece means sitting beneath it. The last F is a border letter and is not clued.
explanation.definitionFit: Mischief once meant harm or evil-doing, a sense kept in phrases such as 'do someone a mischief'.

clue.text: Bowler Hemmings (with England ultimately) spun

parts.note: Eddie Hemmings was an England off-spin bowler of the 1980s

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: the final letter of the country

explanation.surface: A spin bowler who turned the ball for England late in his career.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spun' fits the cricket picture, which hides that it is the definition: water that eddies swirls round.
explanation.definitionFit: To eddy is to move in a circular swirl, like water or smoke turning round and round.

clue.text: One's written in two forms of "Edward" — not changed by publisher

indicators.note: a word written inside another sits within it

parts.note: Ned and Ted are both pet forms of Edward
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A name spelt two ways in a manuscript the publisher left untouched.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening U is a border letter and is not clued. The 's of 'One's' stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: An unedited text is published as it was submitted, with no corrections or revisions.

clue.text: Feeling of disgust upset man — male denied employment

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters are jumbled
what is denied is refused entry, so that letter is struck out

parts.note: man with its M removed
M is the abbreviation for male, the letter taken away
use is employment, as in putting something to use

explanation.surface: A sickened man barred from work because he is male.
explanation.walkthrough: The bottom A is a border letter, so the anagram makes only the first five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Nausea is sickness in the stomach, and figuratively a strong revulsion at something.

clue.text: Study country society

parts.note: Peru is a South American country
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: A survey of rural social life.
explanation.walkthrough: The final E is a border letter and is not clued; 'country society' sounds like rural life, but it is a nation plus an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: To peruse is to read or examine something carefully, the same as studying it.

clue.text: Native American will be upstanding — just some revolutionary

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the letters are read the other way
only some of the words are needed, so the answer is a run of their letters

parts.note: the run of letters straddling the three words

explanation.surface: A call for an indigenous American to stand up, with a hint of rebellion.
explanation.walkthrough: The last O is a border letter, so only five letters are hidden. 'Upstanding' looks like the down-clue reversal signal, but it is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pueblo are Native American peoples of the Southwest, named for their adobe villages.

clue.text: Period of isolation? Auntie ran off

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An aunt who fled to be alone for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: The Q is a border letter, which is why no Q appears in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Quarantine is enforced isolation to stop disease spreading, originally forty days for ships.

clue.text: It's doubly hard jumping across a ditch

indicators.note: leaping across something straddles it, so one piece goes either side of another

parts.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard, taken twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: A steeplechaser finding a wide ditch twice as hard to clear.
explanation.walkthrough: The final A is a border letter. A ha-ha is a sunken ditch with a wall, common on English country estates, which keeps livestock out without blocking the view.
explanation.definitionFit: A ha-ha is a ditch built as a hidden boundary, so the general word covers it.

clue.text: That man and I may expect to inherit

definitions.note: a verb phrase for the person who may expect to inherit

parts.note: he is the pronoun for that man
taken as written

explanation.surface: Two men confidently awaiting a legacy.
explanation.walkthrough: The final R lies on the border and is not clued. The definition describes what the answer does rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: An heir is the person in line to receive an estate or title after the holder dies.

clue.text: Pieces of music? Ecstasy to person entertained no end

indicators.note: having no end means the final letter is dropped

parts.note: E is slang for the drug ecstasy
a guest is someone entertained, here without the final letter

explanation.surface: A party host's musical numbers giving a guest endless ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: The initial S is a border letter and is not clued. The question mark flags a loose definition: segues are transitions between pieces rather than pieces themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A segue is a smooth move from one musical number into the next without a pause.

clue.text: Mice destroyed by what sounds like blunt instrument

indicators.note: this phrase says the word is to be taken by its pronunciation

parts.note: dull means blunt, and is pronounced like the first syllable of the instrument

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken up, so its letters are reassembled differently

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Mice battered to death with a blunt instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blunt instrument' reads as a murder weapon, but the words split: 'blunt' feeds the wordplay and 'instrument' alone defines. The final R is a border letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A dulcimer is a stringed instrument played by striking its strings with small hammers.
